questions.q: You measure the spending of the same 20 customers before and after a loyalty program launch. Which test fits?
options: One-sample t-test against zero dollars
Independent two-sample t-test
Chi-square test
Paired t-test on each customer's change in spend
questions.explain: The measurements are matched by customer, so the paired test analyzes per-customer differences and removes between-customer variation.

questions.q: In the lesson, the same before/after data gave p = 0.0011 when paired and p = 0.2509 when treated as independent. Why?
options: The independent test is always less accurate
Paired tests always give smaller p-values regardless of data
Customer-to-customer differences in spending swamp the change in an independent analysis; pairing removes that variation
The data changed between the two runs
questions.explain: Pairing compares each customer with themselves, so stable differences between customers cancel out.

questions.q: What does equal_var=False in stats.ttest_ind do?
options: Forces both groups to have identical variances
Runs Welch's t-test, which does not assume the two groups have equal variances
Runs a one-sided test
Removes outliers automatically
questions.explain: Welch's version is a safe default when group sizes or spreads differ. scipy's own default is the Student version (equal_var=True).

questions.q: A one-sample test of delivery time against a 3-day promise gives p = 0.0509 at alpha = 0.05. What is the best conclusion?
options: Delivery matches the promise
The sample doesn't quite clear the significance bar; report the estimated difference and its uncertainty rather than declaring no effect
The mean delivery time is exactly 3 days
The test must be rerun until p falls below 0.05
questions.explain: The 0.05 line is a convention. A p just above it is weak-to-moderate evidence, not proof of equality, and rerunning until it passes is p-hacking.

questions.q: When is a one-sided t-test (alternative='greater') appropriate?
options: When the two-sided test wasn't significant
Whenever you expect a positive effect after seeing the data
Only when the direction was decided beforehand and an effect in the other direction would be disregarded
Always, because it has more power
questions.explain: Choosing the direction after seeing the data inflates false alarms. When in doubt, use a two-sided test.
